desc:
A group of n players with skill values skills[i] must be divided into Team A and Team B: every player joins exactly one of the two teams, and either team may be empty. A split is balanced when both teams have the same total skill.

Players are told apart by position, even when their skills are equal, and the teams are labelled, so swapping which team is called A and which is called B gives a different assignment. Return the number of balanced assignments.

For example, [1, 1, 2, 2] has 4 balanced assignments: Team A must hold one player of skill 1 and one of skill 2 (2 × 2 ways), and Team B gets the rest.
hints: Giving every player to A or B is a binary choice per player, so there are 2<sup>n</sup> assignments. With n ≤ 20 that is about a million; can you enumerate them?
Team A and Team B have equal totals exactly when Team A's total is half of the grand total. If the grand total is odd, the answer is 0.
Count the subsets (by position) whose sum is total / 2. A recursion that takes or skips each player works; so does a table ways[s] updated player by player.
editorial: Let total be the sum of all skills. An assignment is balanced exactly when Team A's sum equals total / 2 (then Team B's sum is automatically the same). So the answer is the number of subsets of positions whose sum is total / 2, and it is 0 if total is odd. Because teams are labelled, each such subset is one assignment (A = the subset), and its complement is a different assignment counted separately.

The direct backtracking solution takes or skips each player and counts the paths that end with the target sum: 2<sup>20</sup> leaves at worst. Pruning by the running sum already helps, since all skills are positive.

A faster solution replaces the recursion by a table: ways[s] is the number of subsets seen so far with sum s. For each skill x, update s from high to low with ways[s] += ways[s - x]. The answer is ways[total / 2]. That is O(n · total).
